questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form
questions.problem:
Which of the following matrices are **not** in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${c}_{22}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $C$ is **not** in row echelon form.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Operations That Would Transform a Matrix To Row Echelon Form
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ given below.
Which entries of $A$ could be replaced by $0$ in order to get a matrix in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that by replacing ${a}_{31}$ and ${a}_{42}$ with $0$, we get a matrix in row echelon form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\,⟶\,[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The other options will not give us a matrix in row echelon form.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form
questions.problem:
Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${a}_{45}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $B$ and $C$ are in row echelon form.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Augmented Matrices in Row Echelon Form
questions.problem:
Which of the following augmented matrices are **not** in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 6\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the first row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $A$ is **not** in row echelon form.

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ given below.
Which entries of $A$ could be replaced by $0$ in order to get a matrix in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -3 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that by replacing ${a}_{31}$, ${a}_{32}$ and ${a}_{43}$ with $0$, we get a matrix in row echelon form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -3 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}]\,⟶\,[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

The other options will not give us a matrix in row echelon form.
